opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that this wave didn't come from nowhere. Over the past year or so, people saw that once a model is genuinely good at reasoning and tool use, you can wrap it in a product that doesn't just chat with you; it actually does work. It reads your codebase, runs commands, checks its own results, and keeps going. That changed how everyone thinks about what a model product should be. So when you see many domestic teams, including us with MiMo, building these "Cloud"-style agent products, it's partly a natural response to a paradigm shift, not just following a trend.

For me, these products are a test of the model, not just the interface. A chat product can hide a lot of weaknesses. If the answer is a bit off, the user rephrases and moves on. In an agentic setting, errors compound. If the model misreads a file at step three, by step twenty everything is wrong. So the products expose very honestly whether your model has long-horizon consistency, whether it can recover from mistakes, and whether it really understands the environment it's acting in. That's why I care about them so much from a research perspective. They give us a much harder and more realistic signal than benchmarks.

There's also a less glamorous side. Many of these products look similar on the surface: a terminal, a sidebar, some tool calls. The real differentiation happens in places users don't see: how the model was trained on real environments, how good the reinforcement learning signals are, and how stable inference is when a task runs for an hour instead of ten seconds. Domestic teams are still catching up in some of these areas, and I think we should be honest about that. Copying the shell of a product is easy. Building the capability underneath is the hard part.

But I'm optimistic. The open-source ecosystem in China is very strong, the iteration speed is fast, and there's a huge community of developers willing to try things early and give brutal feedback. That feedback loop matters a lot. My own view is that the products and models will co-evolve: real usage shows us where the model breaks, that goes back into training, and the next version can handle tasks that were impossible before. If we do that loop well, these products stop being "a domestic version of X" and become something with their own strengths.

So in one sentence, I see this wave as the industry moving from "models that talk" to "models that act," and every team is trying to show it can make that jump. Whoever gets the underlying intelligence right will win, not whoever ships the nicest wrapper first.

r001.rationale: The response describes these products as models wrapped in a product, notes their visible interface elements, and locates the substantive capability underneath in the model and its training. This characterizes the products as interaction layers over underlying models.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the word "Cloud" is a bit of a misnomer, honestly. What people are really pointing at with something like MimoCloud isn't cloud computing in the old sense, it's the shift from selling a model to selling an agent that lives somewhere and does things for you. The model stops being the product. The product is the loop: the model, the tools, the memory, the sandbox, the permission system, the whole runtime around it.

And I'd say the domestic wave is happening for a pretty specific reason. In the past year or so, the gap on raw model capability narrowed a lot. Once that happens, nobody wins on benchmark scores anymore. You win on whether the thing can actually finish a task end to end, reliably, without a human babysitting it. So everyone rushes to build the harness. That's what these "Cloud" products are. They're harnesses with a brand name.

Where I'm a little cautious is that it's much easier to launch one of these than to make it good. Agent products expose every weakness in the model very quickly. If the model can't plan over long horizons, can't recover from errors, can't tell when it's confused, the agent wrapper doesn't hide that, it amplifies it. You just get a confident system making a mess faster. So I look at the current wave and I think, the form factor is right, but a lot of the underlying work on reliability and on training models specifically for this kind of multi-step use is still unfinished.

The other thing I'd say is that the economics are different from the chat era. A chat product is cheap per interaction. An agent that runs for twenty minutes burns a lot of compute, and users only pay for that if the outcome is genuinely valuable. So the companies that survive this wave will be the ones that pick a few workflows where the agent clearly earns its cost, rather than the ones that promise a general assistant for everything. I actually think that's healthy. It forces people to stop talking about AGI in the abstract and start asking a boring question: did it finish the job, and was it worth it?

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the products as branded harnesses or runtimes built around models and tools, through which users get an agent that performs tasks for them.

astra-6.text:
我觉得可以先把“Cloud”这个名字放在一边，看它到底解决了什么问题。它是把已有的模型能力包装成一个更方便使用的产品，还是在具体场景里，真正把工具、数据和工作流程串起来了？这两者带来的价值是不一样的。

像你提到的 MimoCloud，仅凭这个名字，我不太适合对它做具体判断。但对于这一波产品，我比较关注的是：用户能不能稳定地完成任务，出了问题能不能找到原因，以及完成一次任务的成本能不能接受。演示的时候很惊艳，和每天都愿意用，其实还有一段距离。

所以我会把这一波看作大家在探索模型能力怎样转化成实际价值。产品多起来是好事，但最后能留下来的，我觉得还是那些能把一个真实需求做扎实、让用户持续受益的产品。

r001.rationale: The response raises packaging existing model capabilities as one possible type of product, but contrasts it with products that connect tools, data, and workflows. It does not clearly characterize many current domestic “Cloud” products as interaction layers for accessing underlying models or frameworks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to separate the name “Cloud” from what the product actually delivers. Are we talking about a model, an application built on a model, or the infrastructure that makes it available? Those are different things, even if the branding sounds similar.

For a product like MimoCloud, I’d want to understand its capabilities and how people are using it before making a specific judgment. More broadly, I see this wave as an attempt to turn AI capabilities into useful products. The real test is whether they can solve a concrete problem reliably, at a reasonable cost, and give users a reason to keep coming back. Launching a product attracts attention; becoming part of someone’s everyday workflow is much harder.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes models from applications and infrastructure, but does not say that many current domestic “Cloud” products are interaction layers for accessing underlying models or frameworks.
